scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The pas de deux originated in the early 18th century as an opening act for operas and ballets.
It evolved through the Baroque period, with ballets like 'The Loves of Mars and Venus' (1717) focusing on dramatic characterization.
Marius Petipa formalized the five-part structure in the 19th century, which remains the standard for the grand pas de deux.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The pas de deux is typically the climax of a scene or an entire ballet, symbolizing romantic love, affection, and the partnership between two characters.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a suite.
The adagio features supported balances, turns, and lifts (portés).
The variations showcase individual athleticism, including pirouettes and leaps.
Watch for Promenade, Portée.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is typically orchestral, composed to support the specific emotional and technical requirements of each section.
The adagio is slow and melodic, while variations and the coda are faster and more rhythmic to accommodate acrobatic movement.
Listen for the Orchestra.
Orchestral music structured to match the five-part dance, moving from slow, lyrical adagio melodies to fast, high-energy climactic codas.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Marius Petipa is the primary figure associated with the codification of the grand pas de deux.
Famous performers include Mikhail Baryshnikov, Gregory Hines, Tamara Rojo, Julio Bocca, Uliana Lopátkina, and Ígor Zelenski.

While the structure is standard in classical ballet, contemporary choreographers like Maurice Béjart, George Balanchine, and Akram Khan have adapted the form for same-sex duos and more acrobatic, non-traditional movements.
Inheritor of the 18th-century 'entrée à deux' and developed through the Romantic ballet of the 19th century.
